Optimized Task Scheduling in Fog-Cloud Computing Using Hybrid Deep Learning and Metaheuristic Algorithms
Amir Heirati1 · Mehdi Fartash1 · Mohammad Khalily-Dermany2
Received: 15 February 2025 / Accepted: 17 November 2025 / Published online: 1 December 2025 © The Author(s) 2025
Abstract Fog computing has emerged as an effective paradigm to address the latency issues inher- ent in cloud computing by enabling data processing closer to data sources, particularly for IoT applications in healthcare, smart transportation, and industrial automation. However, efficient task scheduling in fog environments remains challenging due to their dynamic, het- erogeneous nature. This paper presents an integrated solution for task scheduling in fog-cloud environments to reduce energy consumption and minimize task makespan, while maintaining high-quality service (QoS). The proposed model comprises three core components: work- load prediction, task offloading, and scheduling optimization. First, a Feedforward Neural Network (FNN) is used to predict workload, allowing for proactive resource allocation. Next, a reinforcement learning (RL) model dynamically manages task offloading decisions based on real-time performance metrics, determining whether tasks should be processed on local fog nodes or offloaded to the cloud. Finally, a hybrid optimization algorithm combining Harris Hawk Optimization (HHO) and Genetic Algorithm (GA) refines task scheduling by mapping tasks to available resources efficiently. Simulation results show that the proposed method achieves significant improvements in energy efficiency, reduces task completion times, and enhances QoS metrics compared to baseline scheduling algorithms. The novelty of this work lies in the synergistic integration of predictive deep learning, adaptive RL-based offloading with a multi-objective reward function, and a hybrid HHO-GA optimizer featuring a customizable four-objective fitness function, which collectively address dynamic workload fluctuations and multi-objective trade-offs unmet by existing hybrid methods.
Keywords Fog computing · Task scheduling · Deep learning · Harris Hawk optimization · Genetic algorithm · Reinforcement learning · Quality of service

1 Introduction
Recently, the IoT has emerged as one of the most significant advancements in the field of information technology [1, 2]. The rapid proliferation of IoT devices and the emergence of data-intensive applications have led to an unprecedented surge in data volume and compu- tational demands [3]. This paradigm shift has exposed the limitations of traditional cloud computing in handling real-time applications due to the inherent latency introduced by data transmission to centralized data centers [4]. This latency bottleneck is particularly challeng- ing for applications that demand rapid response times, such as those in healthcare monitoring, emergency response, autonomous vehicles, and industrial automation [5–7].
Fog computing, an extension of cloud computing to the network edge, offers a compelling solution by enabling computation, storage, and networking services closer to data sources and end users [8]. This technology significantly enhances performance and security while reduc- ing latency by positioning computational resources closer to edge devices. Fog computing is particularly impactful in smart cities and healthcare services, serving as an intermediary layer between IoT sensors/devices and centralized cloud data centers. By facilitating more efficient resource provisioning and service administration, fog computing addresses the limitations of traditional cloud computing and supports the increasing demands of real-time applications and large-scale data processing [9, 10].
Cloud environments can significantly bolster IoT communities. Cloud computing is recog- nized as a vast resource hub, enabling universal access to resources for customers efficiently through virtual means. The inherent limitations of current smart devices, such as storage capacity, battery life, network capabilities, and processing power, can be mitigated by offload- ing intensive tasks to robust computing environments like cloud and fog computing. This optimization minimizes time costs while allowing smart devices to handle simpler tasks [11]. Fog computing is a distributed computing paradigm that enhances the functionality of IoT ecosystems. It is distinct in its use of fog nodes—devices that provide access to services, maintain significant data capacity, and facilitate communication. Essentially, fog computing extends cloud computing by distributing digital resources to mobile users. Job scheduling in this context aims to create high-performance, cost-effective fog nodes. Fog computing offers benefits such as reduced latency and decreased network congestion. However, these advantages introduce additional challenges in task scheduling and resource allocation [12, 13]. Fog computing offers numerous benefits such as reduced latency, bandwidth savings, location awareness, and enhanced security and privacy. However, these advantages come with the complexity of managing and scheduling tasks efficiently across heterogeneous fog nodes to meet dynamic user requirements. Processing data closer to its source significantly reduces the time required to transmit data to centralized servers and receive results, enabling real-time or near-real-time application performance [14–16]. Local processing in fog nodes alleviates the burden on network bandwidth, as only essential data needs to be transmitted to the cloud [17]. This is particularly beneficial for IoT applications that generate large volumes of data [18]. Fog computing inherently incorporates location information, enabling context- aware applications that leverage the proximity of fog nodes to users and data sources [19]. Processing sensitive data locally in fog nodes reduces the risk of data breaches and privacy violations, as data is not necessarily transmitted to centralized servers. This is especially important for applications handling personal health information, financial data, and other confidential information [20].

In fog computing, resources are distributed across a network of fog nodes, including gateways, routers, access points, and even end devices with sufficient computational capa- bilities [21]. This distributed architecture allows for more efficient resource utilization and a reduction in the reliance on centralized cloud infrastructure. However, the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of fog environments introduces several challenges for efficient task scheduling. Fluctuating workloads make it difficult to anticipate resource demands and allo- cate them efficiently [22]. This variability arises from the diverse nature of IoT applications, user behavior, and environmental factors. Resource heterogeneity adds complexity to the task allocation process, as fog nodes differ in their computational capabilities, energy efficiency, and communication bandwidth [23]. This heterogeneity makes it crucial to select the most suitable fog node for each task based on its specific requirements. Real-time applications have strict latency requirements, demanding that tasks be completed within specific dead- lines [24]. Failing to meet these deadlines can have significant consequences, particularly in safety–critical applications. Minimizing energy consumption is essential in fog comput- ing, especially for fog nodes operating on limited power sources [25]. Balancing energy efficiency with performance is a key challenge in resource allocation. Achieving a balance between minimizing makespan, energy consumption, cost, and ensuring high QoS involves optimizing multiple conflicting objectives; for instance, allocating tasks to the fastest fog nodes might reduce makespan but increase energy consumption or cost [26].
Traditional task scheduling algorithms often struggle to address these challenges, espe- cially when considering multiple objectives simultaneously [27]. This paper proposes a novel task scheduling approach that combines deep learning, reinforcement learning, and a hybrid optimization algorithm to overcome these limitations and achieve efficient and adaptive resource allocation in a collaborative fog-cloud environment. Deep learning excels in pat- tern recognition, predicting resource demands, and identifying optimal scheduling patterns based on historical data. Reinforcement learning adapts scheduling strategies to optimize performance metrics in real-time. The hybrid optimization algorithm enhances the global optimization and local fine-tuning of the scheduling strategy. This synergistic combination ensures a robust and adaptive solution, capable of handling the complexities of a collaborative fog-cloud environment.
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
• A Novel Integrated Framework: We propose a three-stage hybrid model that sequentially integrates workload prediction (FNN), dynamic task offloading (RL), and multi-objective task scheduling (HHO-GA). This holistic approach addresses the scheduling problem from prediction to execution, a gap not fully covered by existing methods. • Proactive and Adaptive Scheduling: By combining FNN for future workload prediction with an RL agent for real-time offloading decisions, our model moves beyond reactive scheduling. It proactively allocates resources and dynamically adapts to changing network conditions, significantly improving efficiency and QoS. • Advanced Multi-Objective Optimization: The hybridization of Harris Hawk Optimization (HHO) for global exploration and a Genetic Algorithm (GA) for local solution refine- ment creates a powerful optimizer. This combination effectively balances the conflicting objectives of minimizing energy consumption, makespan, and SLA violations, while max- imizing resource utilization. • Superior Performance: Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art algorithms across key perfor- mance metrics, validating its effectiveness and practical applicability for demanding IoT applications.

2 Literature Review
The field of task scheduling in cloud and fog computing has been extensively studied, with a wide range of algorithms proposed to address various challenges, such as latency, energy efficiency, and resource utilization. These algorithms can be broadly categorized into tra- ditional, heuristic, metaheuristic, machine learning, and hybrid approaches, as summarized in Table 1. Each category offers unique strengths, such as simplicity in traditional methods or adaptability in machine learning, but also faces limitations, particularly in handling the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of fog-cloud environments. This section reviews these categories in detail, highlighting their mechanisms, applications, and gaps that the proposed method aims to address.

TheseincludesimpleschedulingtechniqueslikeRoundRobin(RR),First-Come-First-Served (FCFS), Shortest Job First (SJF), and Earliest Deadline First (EDF). While easy to imple- ment, these algorithms often fail to consider the complexities of cloud-fog environments, neglecting factors such as resource heterogeneity, energy consumption, and dynamic work- load fluctuations [28].

2.2 Heuristic Approaches
Heuristic algorithms, aim to find good solutions in a reasonable time but do not guarantee optimality. These methods typically employ priority rules or greedy strategies to assign tasks to resources, focusing on minimizing makespan or maximizing resource utilization. However, they often struggle to handle multiple conflicting objectives effectively [29].
2.3 Metaheuristic Algorithms
Metaheuristic algorithms, inspired by natural processes, offer powerful techniques for solving complex optimization problems. Examples include:
• Genetic Algorithm (GA): Mimics the process of natural selection, iteratively improving a population of candidate solutions through crossover and mutation operations [30]. • Ant Colony Optimization (ACO): Simulates the foraging behavior of ants, using pheromone trails to guide the search for optimal solutions. • Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO): Inspired by the flocking behavior of birds, particles representing candidate solutions move through the search space, guided by their own best solution and the best solution found by the swarm. • Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO): Mimics the hunting behavior of grey wolves, with solutions representing wolves searching for prey (optimal solution).
Metaheuristicalgorithmshaveshownpromiseinoptimizingtaskschedulingformakespan, energy consumption, and cost. However, they can suffer from slow convergence, local optima traps, and a lack of solution diversity, especially in highly dynamic environments [31].
2.4 Machine Learning Approaches
Machine learning techniques have gained significant traction in recent years for intelligent task scheduling in cloud-fog environments. These methods leverage data-driven models to learn patterns and make predictions, Deep Q-Learning (DQL): Combines deep neural net- works with Q-learning, a reinforcement learning technique, to learn optimal policies for task scheduling, aiming to maximize long-term rewards based on observed system states and actions [28, 32].
• Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL): Employs more sophisticated neural network architectures and learning algorithms to handle complex tasks and dynamic environments [33].
ML approaches offer the potential for adaptive and self-optimizing scheduling solutions. However, they require substantial training data and can be computationally intensive, partic- ularly in complex scenarios [34].
2.5 Hybrid Approaches
Recognizing the strengths and limitations of different techniques, hybrid approaches have emerged, combining the benefits of metaheuristic algorithms, machine learning, and other methods. These approaches aim to leverage the strengths of each technique to overcome the limitations of individual methods. For instance, a hybrid approach could use DRL to predict

3 Methods
This section presents the proposed task scheduling method for a collaborative fog-cloud computing environment. The aim is to optimize resource utilization, minimize energy con- sumption, and ensure timely task execution for real-time applications. The method consists of three main stages: workload prediction using deep learning, task offloading decisions based on reinforcement learning, and task scheduling optimization using a hybrid HHO and GA approach.

The algorithm integrates three stages—Workload Prediction, Task Offloading, and Task Scheduling—to optimize resource allocation in dynamic fog-cloud environments. Below, each stage is described with practical examples and design rationales, ensuring clarity for readers unfamiliar with deep learning or metaheuristic techniques (See Algorithm 1).
• Stage 1: Workload Prediction (Lines 1–7)
This stage uses a Feedforward Neural Network (FNN) to forecast the next hour’s workload based on 24-h historical data. Historical user requests (e.g., 450 requests/second at 8 PM) are collected (Line 2) and preprocessed into five categories (Very Low: <100, Low: 100–300, Medium: 300–500, High: 500–700, Very High: >700) to simplify input for the FNN (Line 3). The FNN, initialized with 24 input neurons (one per hour), two hidden layers (64 and 32 neurons with ReLU activation for non-linear pattern detection), and one output neuron (Line 4), is trained on this data (Line 5). For example, if past data shows a peak of 650 requests at 9 AM, the FNN predicts a High workload (e.g., 550 requests) for 10 AM (Line 6). This prediction enables proactive scaling of fog nodes, reducing bottlenecks by allocating resources before demand spikes.
• Stage 2: Task Offloading (Lines 8–15)
A Reinforcement Learning (RL) agent with Q-learning determines whether tasks are executed locally on fog nodes or offloaded to the cloud. Initialized with a Q-table (Line 9), the agent evaluates the system state (e.g., fog node at 70% capacity, predicted workload of 500 requests) for each task (Line 11). It selects an action—local execution or cloud offload—based on the Q-table’s policy (Line 12). The reward function (Eq. 1) balances completion time, energy consumption, and a deadline bonus (Line 13). For instance, a healthcare monitoring task with a 4-s deadline might yield a reward of + 10 for local execution (3 s, low energy) versus + 5 for cloud offload (2 s, higher energy). The Q-table updates using a learning rate (α  0.1) and discount factor (γ  0.9) to prioritize long-term efficiency (Line 14). This stage ensures adaptive decisions, optimizing for latency-sensitive IoT applications like smart transportation.
• Stage 3: Task Scheduling (Lines 16–29)
This stage maps tasks to resources using a hybrid Harris Hawk Optimization (HHO) and Genetic Algorithm (GA). HHO initializes a population of schedules (Line 18) and iterates up to 100 times (Line 19). In exploration, hawks (schedules) perch randomly to diversify solu- tions (e.g., reassigning tasks from an overloaded node), while in exploitation, they encircle the best schedule to refine it (Line 20). Fitness is evaluated using Eq. 3, balancing energy consumption (e.g., 200 MJ), makespan (e.g., 50 s), SLA violations (e.g., 10 s), and resource utilization (e.g., 80%) with tunable weights (w1–w4, e.g., 0.3, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2) (Line 21). After HHO, the best schedule is refined by GA (Line 24). GA applies crossover (e.g., swapping task assignments between two schedules to reduce makespan by 10%) and mutation (e.g., reassigning one task to balance load) over 100 iterations (Lines 25–27). The final sched- ule (Line 29) minimizes energy and latency while maximizing QoS, suitable for dynamic fog-cloud systems.

3.1 Workload Prediction using Deep Learning
Accurate workload prediction is crucial for efficient resource allocation. We use a FNN to forecast incoming user requests for various fog brokers based on historical usage patterns.
3.1.1 Data Preprocessing and Categorization
Data on user request patterns are collected over specific time windows and preprocessed to create suitable inputs for the FNN. The number of requests per second is categorized into five nominal ranges: Very Low, Low, Medium, High, and Very High (see Table 2).
3.1.2 FNN Architecture
Our FNN architecture is designed with a specific structure to effectively capture and predict user request patterns. The architecture is as follows:

• Input Layer: Comprising 24 neurons, this layer processes hourly collected workload data over the past 24 h, providing a time-series input to the network. • Hidden Layer 1: Featuring 64 neurons, this layer employs the ReLU activation function to learn complex patterns and relationships within the workload data. • Hidden Layer 2: With 32 neurons, this layer further refines the representations captured by the first hidden layer, also utilizing the ReLU activation function to extract higher-level abstractions. • Output Layer: Consisting of a single neuron with a linear activation function, this layer outputs the predicted workload for the next hour.
This architecture, with two hidden layers and a decreasing number of neurons, is specif- ically designed to progressively extract and refine meaningful features from the input data, optimizing the model’s predictive accuracy.
3.2 Task Offloading Decision Using Reinforcement Learning
To efficiently utilize both fog and cloud resources, an intelligent offloading mechanism is essential. This stage leverages Q-learning, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) algo- rithm, to dynamically determine whether a task should be executed locally on a fog node or offloaded to the cloud server.
The fog-cloud environment is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where each state represents the current workload distribution across fog nodes and the cloud. The RL agent’s actions are to decide whether to offload a task or execute it locally.
3.2.1 Reward Function
The reward function guides the agent to learn an optimal policy that minimizes both task completion time and energy consumption:
Reward(s, a)  completion_ time(task, a) −energy_ consumption(task, a) + bonus (1)
where:
• s is the current state (workload distribution). • a is the action taken (offload or local execution). • completion_ time(task, a) is the estimated completion time for the task given the action. • energy_ consumption(task, a) is the estimated energy consumption for the task given the action. • A bonus is provided if the task meets its deadline on a fog node to encourage local pro- cessing when feasible.

3.3 Hybrid Optimization for Task Scheduling
Once offloading decisions are made, tasks assigned to both fog nodes and the cloud must be scheduled optimally. We achieve this by combining the strengths of the HHO algorithm [36] and the GA in a powerful hybrid approach. This approach identifies the best possible mapping of tasks to available resources (fog nodes or cloud VMs) while considering multiple objectives.
3.3.1 HHO
HHO simulates the cooperative hunting behavior of Harris hawks. Each hawk represents a potential solution, which is a schedule that assigns tasks to specific resources. The algorithm iteratively improves these solutions over multiple iterations.
• Exploration: Hawks randomly perch based on their knowledge of the prey’s location and the positions of other hawks. This exploration phase helps to diversify the search and avoid local optima. • Exploitation: Hawks encircle and attack the prey based on its escaping energy. This phase focuses on exploiting promising regions of the search space to refine the solutions. • Transition: A parameter controls the gradual transition from exploration to exploitation as the algorithm progresses, balancing global and local search.
3.3.2 GA
After a predefined number of HHO iterations, the best solution (task schedule) obtained is further refined using GA operators.
• Crossover: Combines parts of two parent solutions (schedules) to create new offspring solutions, potentially inheriting good traits from both parents. • Mutation: Introduces small random changes to the solutions to maintain diversity and prevent premature convergence to suboptimal schedules (see Fig. 2).

3.3.3 Fitness Function
The fitness function (Eq. 3) combines four objectives weighted by w1, w2, w3, w4 where w1 +w2 +w3 +w4  1 and 0 ≤wi ≤1. Specifically, w1 prioritizes minimizing EnergyCon- sumption (energy used by fog nodes/cloud VMs),w2 emphasizes reducing CompletionTime (makespan), w3 focuses on minimizing SLAviolation (deadline violations), and w4 promotes maximizing ResourceUtilization (efficient resource use). EnergyConsumption is measured in watt-hours, CompletionTime and SLAviolation in seconds, and ResourceUtilization as a normalized ratio (0–1). These weights allow flexible tuning to meet application-specific needs, such as prioritizing energy efficiency for battery-powered fog nodes or low latency for real-time IoT tasks.

By combining HHO and GA, the proposed method effectively explores the search space, identifies promising solutions, and fine-tunes them to achieve high-quality task schedules that balance performance and QoS in fog-cloud computing environments.

4 Results and Discussion
This section evaluates the performance of the proposed hybrid task scheduling method, integrating FNN, RL, and HHO and GA, against state-of-the-art algorithms in fog-cloud com- puting. The primary baseline is the Multi-Objective Grey Wolf Optimizer (MGWO) [37], with additional comparisons against Zhou et al. [38], AFED-EF [39], and IADE [40]. The exper- iments, conducted using MATLAB R2024a, assess six key metrics: Energy Consumption, Makespan (task completion time), Scheduling Time, Percentage of Tasks Completed within Deadlines, Deadline Violation Time, and Energy Efficiency.These metrics evaluate efficiency, responsiveness, and Quality of Service (QoS) under varying service loads (200–600 tasks). The following subsections detail the simulation environment, results, and comparative anal- ysis, demonstrating the proposed method’s superiority in dynamic resource provisioning.
The proposed method’s performance improvements—reducing energy consumption by 2–11%, task completion time by at least 30%, and computational overhead (5.7 vs. 6.4) compared to the MGWO baseline [37]—have significant implications for fog-cloud comput- ing applications. These gains enhance system scalability and energy efficiency, critical for real-time IoT applications such as healthcare monitoring, smart transportation, and industrial automation. For instance, reduced energy consumption lowers operational costs and environ- mental impact, while shorter completion times improve user satisfaction in latency-sensitive scenarios. The higher percentage of tasks completed within deadlines (2–4% improvement) and lower SLA violation times ensure better QoS, making the proposed method suitable for safety–critical systems. To assess the statistical significance of these improvements, a paired t-test was conducted on key metrics (energy consumption, task completion time, computa- tional overhead, percentage of tasks completed within deadlines, and SLA violation time) across service ranges (200–600). The results yielded p-values < 0.05 for all metrics, con- firming that the improvements over the baseline are statistically significant. This analysis underscores the robustness of the proposed method, attributing its success to the synergistic integration of FNN-based workload prediction, RL-based offloading, and hybrid HHO-GA optimization. These findings suggest that the method can be practically deployed in dynamic fog computing environments to achieve cost-effective, high-performance task scheduling.
4.1 Simulation Environment and Parameters
The simulations were conducted using MATLAB R2024a on a desktop computer equipped with an Intel Core i7-8700 processor (3.2 GHz), 16 GB of RAM, and the Windows 10 (64- bit) operating system. The fog-cloud environment was modeled with configurations detailed in Table 3, including fog node specifications (e.g., CPU frequency, memory capacity) and task characteristics (e.g., task size, deadlines). This setup ensured sufficient computational resources for accurate and reproducible simulation results.
The proposed method’s performance is evaluated using five key metrics: energy con- sumption of fog cells, task completion time, computational overhead, percentage of tasks completed within the deadline, and total SLA violation time. The results are then compared with the baseline approach.

4.3 Comparative Analysis
This section benchmarks the proposed task scheduling method against prominent approaches in fog computing, highlighting its unique contributions and advantages. Table 5 provides a concise comparison, focusing on key features and performance metrics.
The proposed method offers several key advantages over existing techniques:
• Proactive Resource Allocation: The use of an FNN for workload prediction enables proactive resource provisioning. This foresight allows for more efficient resource utiliza- tion and can prevent bottlenecks, a capability lacking in most compared methods. • Adaptive Task Offloading: The reinforcement learning (RL)-based task offloading mech- anism dynamically adapts to the fog-cloud environment. By learning from real-time performance feedback, the proposed method makes intelligent offloading decisions, opti- mizing both completion time and energy consumption. This contrasts with the static or less adaptable offloading approaches seen in other methods. • Multi-Objective Optimization: The hybrid HHO-GA algorithm effectively tackles the challengeofbalancingmultiple,oftenconflictingobjectives(energy,makespan,QoS).This provides a more comprehensive and practical approach compared to methods optimizing for single objectives. • Balanced Task Distribution: The results highlight the proposed method’s ability to dis- tribute tasks efficiently across available resources. This balanced approach minimizes task completion time and enhances overall system performance. • Addresses Key Gaps: The proposed method directly addresses the weaknesses observed in other approaches, particularly the lack of workload prediction and static offloading decisions. By incorporating these features, it offers a more robust and responsive solution for dynamic fog environments.

5 Conclusion
This study proposes a task scheduling framework (RL + HHOGA) for fog-cloud environ- ments, integrating Feedforward Neural Network (FNN), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and a hybrid Harris Hawk Optimization (HHO) and Genetic Algorithm (GA). Simulations show that RL + HHOGA reduces energy consumption (6.31–12.55%), makespan (38.64–54.85%), and SLA violation time (52.63–63.41%) while improving deadline satisfaction (3.4–8%) compared to baselines like MGWO, Zhou2018, AFED-EF, and IADE. The framework enhances QoS for IoT applications like healthcare and smart transportation. future work could explore advanced ML models and real-world deployments to further optimize perfor- mance.

equations.raw_extracted: A Reinforcement Learning (RL) agent with Q-learning determines whether tasks are executed locally on fog nodes or offloaded to the cloud. Initialized with a Q-table (Line 9), the agent evaluates the system state (e.g., fog node at 70% capacity, predicted workload of 500 requests) for each task (Line 11). It selects an action—local execution or cloud offload—based on the Q-table’s policy (Line 12). The reward function (Eq. 1) balances completion time, energy consumption, and a deadline bonus (Line 13). For instance, a healthcare monitoring task with a 4-s deadline might yield a reward of + 10 for local execution (3 s, low energy) versus + 5 for cloud offload (2 s, higher energy). The Q-table updates using a learning rate (α  0.1) and discount factor (γ  0.9) to prioritize long-term efficiency (Line 14). This stage ensures adaptive decisions, optimizing for latency-sensitive IoT applications like smart transportation.
Reward(s, a)  completion_ time(task, a) −energy_ consumption(task, a) + bonus (1)

• a is the learning rate (0 < a < 1). • γ is the discount factor (0 < γ < 1) that balances immediate and future rewards. • s′ is the next state after taking action a in state s. • a′ represents all possible actions in state s′.

The fitness function (Eq. 3) combines four objectives weighted by w1, w2, w3, w4 where w1 +w2 +w3 +w4  1 and 0 ≤wi ≤1. Specifically, w1 prioritizes minimizing EnergyCon- sumption (energy used by fog nodes/cloud VMs),w2 emphasizes reducing CompletionTime (makespan), w3 focuses on minimizing SLAviolation (deadline violations), and w4 promotes maximizing ResourceUtilization (efficient resource use). EnergyConsumption is measured in watt-hours, CompletionTime and SLAviolation in seconds, and ResourceUtilization as a normalized ratio (0–1). These weights allow flexible tuning to meet application-specific needs, such as prioritizing energy efficiency for battery-powered fog nodes or low latency for real-time IoT tasks.
